children: Kenya is quietly exploring alternative protectionist measures to shield its domestic sugar sub-sector from a potential deluge of cheap imports from the Comesa region in the wake of its exit from the 24-year sugar safeguard regime.

The long-standing protective cushion, which officially lapsed on November 30, 2025, allowed Nairobi to impose strict import quotas on sugar originating from the 21-member Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (Comesa) trading bloc.

Kenya’s Investment Trade and Industry ministry says it is mulling a fresh diplomatic engagement with the Comesa secretariat to negotiate alternative protections to shield the country’s sugar subsector, which is still considered infant compared to other sugar producers from Comesa.

Cabinet Secretary Lee Kinyanjui says the government is looking for a “win-win” solution to protect its sugar sub-sector from the cheap Comesa imports while at the same time living up to the spirit of the Comesa bloc, hinting at the possibility of having a quota arrangement, with key Comesa-based producers.
The minister declined to disclose details of the planned protectionist measures but hinted at the possibility of Comesa member states being given leeway to export their sugar outside the region.

Mr Kinyanjui said there are also discussions on the possibility of Comesa member countries diversifying their sugar export markets outside the bloc to countries as far as the Middle and Far East.“There are countries that have more established industries so that simply means that their cost of production is much lower than ours. If we allowed a free run, it would ‘whitewash’ us. So, we are trying to look for a win-win situation. That is work in progress,” Mr Kinyanjui told The EastAfrican on phone.“Not all countries in Comesa produce sugar. Uganda is now turning out to be a major sugar-manufacturing country. May be to look for possibility of having a quota arrangement, but we have not made any decision. We are reviewing to look at the impact of Kenya’s sugar industry vis-a-vis our Comesa engagement.”“As a country we have to establish our volumes, then after establishing our volumes we project what kind of deficit or surplus we have and how we will work on it. It is not good for me to pre-empt what we are likely to do because sugar is a global commodity so, assuming we get to surplus – which we think will happen in the next two years – we are also discussing how the region (Comesa) can be a net exporter. It doesn’t mean Comesa sugar can only be used within Comesa.”
The policy shift followed objections by some Comesa member states to the attempt to prolong the tariff safeguards for Kenya’s sugar industry.
The decision abolished Kenya’s 350,000-tonne annual quota—the maximum amount of duty-free sugar the country had been allowed to import from Comesa to bridge its production deficit.
The quota had been granted to shield Kenya’s less efficient sugar industry from cheaper imports while reforms were implemented to improve competitiveness.

.“The remaining condition for the extension of the safeguards was divestiture from public mills, and you are aware that it has now been achieved after we leased out the mills in May (2025). Considering the divestiture, the mills are now more efficient and we also have two mills coming into operation in March (2026). I’m confident that we are on course to attain domestic self-sufficiency in about two years.”Since 2001, Kenya had relied on Comesa safeguards—renewed eight times—to protect its high-cost domestic sugar industry. Under the arrangement, Kenya could import up to 350,000 tonnes annually from Comesa to bridge the supply deficits. Most imports originated from Mauritius, Uganda, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, India, Brazil, Thailand and Eswatini.
